name: FLORES-101
description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and professionally translated into 101 languages. The sentences cover a variety of topics and domains, sourced from Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage. All translations are multilingually aligned, enabling evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems across 10,100 language pairs.
creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan (Facebook AI Research, LORIA)
inLanguage: 101 languages including English, Spanish, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, and 94 others
citeAs: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan. 2021. The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193v1 [cs.CL]
rai:dataCollection: Sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia, specifically from three sources: Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (age-appropriate nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guides). For each source, articles were selected at random, and 3-5 contiguous sentences were manually selected from each article. Selection was performed by 10 annotators with different roles and geographic backgrounds. Paragraphs were sampled equally from the beginning, middle, and end of articles to avoid bias from document structure.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: All source sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia, including Wikinews (collection of international news articles), Wikijunior (collection of age-appropriate nonfiction books for children from birth to age 12), and WikiVoyage (travel guide with articles about travel tips, food and destinations around the globe). A third of sentences came from each source.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The sentence selection process consisted of selecting an article at random from each source, and then manually selecting a few (typically between 3 and 5) contiguous sentences from each article, avoiding segments with very short or malformed sentences. To avoid bias from document structure, one paragraph per document was selected from either the beginning, middle or end of the article, with roughly one third of paragraphs sampled from each location. For each sentence, Wikipedia URL, topic, and boolean flags indicating whether the sentence contained entities linked to other Wikipedia pages and images were extracted. All sentences were manually labeled by sub-topic (one of 10 possibilities: crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, and travel).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: All source sentences were professionally translated from English into 101 languages by Language Service Providers (LSPs). The translation workflow included: (1) translation by an initial LSP, (2) editing by different translators within the LSP, (3) automated quality control checks (language identification, checking for copied source sentences, length differences, fluency checks via language models, and checking for verbatim copies from commercial translation engines), (4) quality assurance by an independent LSP that provided a translation quality score (0-100 scale) based on identified errors (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register), and (5) re-translation if the quality score was below 90%. The process could repeat for multiple rounds until the 90% quality threshold was met. Two translation LSPs were selected based on pilot experiments evaluating translation quality across multiple providers.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed through a Translation Quality Score calculated per language on a 0 to 100 scale, determined based on the number of identified errors by evaluation LSPs. Errors were examined across categories (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register), each associated with a severity level (minor, major, or critical). The acceptable translation quality score was set to 90%. The largest error category across all languages was mistranslation. All 101 languages in FLORES-101 met the 90% quality threshold, with about 50% of languages achieving quality above 95%.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each sentence received one professional translation per target language, with editing by different translators within the LSP, followed by quality assessment by an independent LSP.
rai:annotatorDemographics: The sentence selection process was performed by 10 different annotators in the research lab: 6 male and 4 female, with different roles in research (researchers including scientists and engineers, and program/project managers), originally coming from different regions of the world (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America and North America). Professional translators were employed through Language Service Providers for the 101 target languages.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables better assessment of model quality on the long tail of low-resource languages and supports evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation systems. The majority of the world's population speak low-resource languages and would benefit from improvements in translation quality on their native languages. By publicly releasing such a high-quality and high-coverage dataset, the authors hope to foster progress in the machine translation community and beyond.
rai:dataBiases: All source sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into other languages by human translators. While translationese (overly literal or awkward translations) has known idiosyncrasies, the authors conjecture that these effects are rather marginal when evaluating models in low-resource languages, where current MT systems produce many severe mistakes. The authors believe the benefits of many-to-many evaluation largely outsize the risk of evaluating translationese. The dataset only evaluates translations from English source sentences, which may not fully represent natural text in the target languages.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to evaluation purposes and consists of only 3001 sentences, which may not be sufficient for training machine translation models. All source sentences are in English and translated to other languages, meaning evaluation of non-English source directions involves translationese. The dataset covers broad topics but may not represent all domains or specialized content. Some language pairs have very limited training data available (less than 100K sentences), making translation particularly challenging. Performance varies significantly by language family and resource level, with very low performance (below 5 spBLEU) for many African language families (Bantu, Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, and Nilotic).
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluation of machine translation systems, particularly for low-resource and multilingual translation. It supports evaluation of many-to-many translation (10,100 language pairs), document-level translation (multiple contiguous sentences from the same article), and multimodal translation (sentences with associated images and Wikipedia URLs). The dataset includes three splits: dev (997 sentences for hyperparameter tuning), devtest (1012 sentences for testing during development), and test (992 sentences available only through an evaluation server to prevent overfitting). Beyond translation, FLORES-101 can be used to evaluate tasks such as sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation.
